article.title: UC Berkeley's 48-Sensor Computational Microscope Captures 25.2 Billion Pixels Per Second, Tracks Live C. elegans
article.summary: A UC Berkeley-led team built a computational microscope combining 48 sensors and a diffractive phase mask to hit 25.2 billion pixels per second.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A UC Berkeley-led team of researchers has built a computational microscope that captures 25.2 billion pixels per second, achieving 3-micron resolution across 5 square centimeters at 120 frames per second, according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/). The device, described in a study published in Nature Photonics, is designed to sidestep a long-standing trade-off in microscope design between imaging speed, field of view, and resolution, as [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/) reports: "When designing microscopes, optical engineers have long faced a trade-off between speed, field of view and resolution. But improving one of these properties typically comes at the expense of another."

## What We Know

- The system is built around an array of 48 camera sensors mounted on a credit-card-sized circuit board, according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/) and independently confirmed by [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html).
- Laura Waller, a UC Berkeley professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences and the study's principal investigator, said: "This is really a breakthrough in the field of computational microscopy. With our microscope, we were able to achieve 3-micron resolution across 5 square centimeters at 120 frames per second, which isn't possible with traditional ways," according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).
- Waller also described the achievement as "the largest space-bandwidth time product of any practical microscope we know of," a quote reported by both [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/) and [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html).
- The imaging gain comes from a custom-designed diffractive optical element, or phase mask. Waller explained: "Specifically, we fabricated a custom-designed phase mask — a glass plate that diffracts light in the microscope — so that light that would normally fall between the sensors is redirected onto them instead," as reported by [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).
- A computational algorithm then reconstructs the full image from the compressed sensor data, a mechanism confirmed independently by [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html), which reported that the mask "redirects light that would normally fall between the sensors" onto them, after which "a computational algorithm then reconstructs the complete image from this compressed data."
- Chaoying Gu, a UC Berkeley Ph.D. student in Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences, said the approach removes a common bottleneck: "I think calibration-free capabilities like our method will prove to be one of the key ingredients for scaling up imaging systems in the future," according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).
- The team demonstrated the microscope by tracking dozens of freely moving *C. elegans* nematodes, imaging both their movement and internal structures. Kevin C. Zhou, the study's lead author, said: "The simultaneous high-resolution, wide-field-of-view, high-speed capabilities of our computational microscope allowed us to track the freely moving C. elegans, as well as some structures within them," according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/). [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html) independently reported the same demonstration, including that the team imaged the worms' "pharyngeal pumping" feeding behavior.
- Zhou was formerly a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley and is now an assistant professor at the University of Michigan, according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/) and [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html).
- The project drew collaborators beyond Berkeley: Muneki Ikeda and Saul Kato of UC San Francisco, Tina M. Hayward and Rajesh Menon of the University of Utah, Nicholas Antipa of UC San Diego, and Roarke Horstmeyer of Duke University and Ramona Optics, per [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).
- Funding came from the Office of Naval Research, the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, the National Institutes of Health, the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science, the Schmidt Science Fellows program in partnership with the Rhodes Trust, and the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub SF, according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).
- Waller pointed to further applications ahead: "Our approach could be used to image many live organisms simultaneously and to monitor samples over time," and added, "There's a lot of progress being made, and still to be made, on very large-scale video microscopy. Our study shows that computational imaging — the joint design of hardware and software — has a lot to offer in scaling up to large data acquisition," according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/).

## What We Don't Know

- The underlying Nature Photonics paper itself was not directly accessible for this article — its page returned an authentication redirect rather than article text — so this report relies on the UC Berkeley College of Engineering release and Phys.org's independent coverage of it rather than the primary manuscript. Readers can consult the paper directly via its [DOI record](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41566-026-01974-4).
- Neither source specifies a timeline for commercializing the system or deploying it outside the lab, nor whether the 15-second *C. elegans* demonstration reflects the system's maximum continuous recording duration.
- Cost, manufacturing complexity, and how readily the 48-sensor/phase-mask design could scale to other imaging applications beyond the nematode demonstration were not detailed in the available coverage.

## Analysis

The result adds to a body of "computational imaging" work that treats hardware and reconstruction software as a single system rather than separate stages — an approach the Berkeley team frames explicitly as the source of its gain, with Waller noting the study demonstrates that "computational imaging — the joint design of hardware and software — has a lot to offer in scaling up to large data acquisition," according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/). By using a phase mask to spread light across gaps between discrete sensors and then computationally reconstructing the image, the team sidesteps the physical constraints that force conventional microscope designs to trade off resolution, field of view, and speed against one another. The calibration-free design Gu described could matter for scaling: instruments that need manual calibration each time they're assembled or adjusted are harder to reproduce and deploy at scale than ones that reconstruct images algorithmically from raw sensor data.
